nameStory: Aldrich's Harvestman is named after a scientist who studied these fascinating arachnids, following the traditional practice of honoring researchers who contributed to our understanding of species. The common name "harvestman" comes from the fact that these long-legged creatures are most commonly seen during harvest time in late summer and fall, when they emerge in large numbers.
description: Aldrich's Harvestman is a delicate-looking arachnid with an oval body and extremely long, thin legs that can span several inches. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused together into what looks like a single oval pill, and they don't spin webs or have venom. Their body is typically small - about the size of a pea - but those spindly legs make them appear much larger as they carefully pick their way across surfaces.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Single oval body segment that feels firm to the touch, unlike spiders which have a distinct waist between body parts

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Eight extremely long, thread-like legs that feel delicate and may detach if handled - they continue twitching even when separated from the body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body about pea-sized but leg span can reach 2-3 inches, giving them a spidery appearance from a distance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive swaying, careful gait and often found in groups, especially around damp areas or under logs

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two small eyes positioned on a small bump or turret on top of the body, much less prominent than spider eyes

habitat: Look for Aldrich's Harvestman in moist woodland areas throughout New England, particularly under logs, rocks, and leaf litter where humidity stays high. They're often found near streams, in basement window wells, or crawling on the sides of buildings at night. Unlike many harvestmen, they seem comfortable in both forested areas and suburban gardens with good ground cover.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging as weather warms, often found under overwintering shelter like logs and stone walls.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, often seen climbing on vegetation and building walls at dusk.
seasonality.fall: Most commonly encountered during harvest season, with large aggregations sometimes forming under favorable shelter.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off but eggs overwinter in soil and leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: When threatened, harvestmen can intentionally detach their legs, which continue to twitch and jerk for several minutes - this "zombie leg" keeps predators distracted while the harvestman escapes, though unlike lizard tails, the legs never grow back!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for spiders due to their eight legs, but remember the simple rule: harvestmen have "one body, spiders have two" - if you can see a distinct waist, it's a spider. Harvestmen also can't bite and don't make webs.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "daddy longlegs" like some spiders and crane flies, harvestmen aren't spiders at all - they're more closely related to scorpions and belong to their own order called Opiliones, which means "shepherd" in Latin, referring to their long legs like a shepherd's stilts.
compareHints: Aldrich's Harvestman is very difficult to distinguish from its close relatives like the Eastern Harvestman without examining fine details under magnification. In general, Leiobunum species all share the same basic body plan with smooth, oval bodies and extremely long legs. The best approach for casual observers is to appreciate them as part of the diverse Leiobunum group rather than trying to identify the exact species.
